prompt: According to Table 9.10.1, what happens to a covalent bond as its bond order goes up from 1 to 3?

choices.text: It gets shorter and stronger
It gets longer and stronger
choices.why: Stronger is right, but the bond gets shorter: C–C is 1.54 Å and C≡C is 1.20 Å. More shared electrons hold the nuclei closer together.

choices.text: It gets shorter and weaker
choices.why: Shorter is right, but the bond enthalpy rises: from 348 kJ/mol for C–C to 839 kJ/mol for C≡C.

choices.text: It gets longer and weaker
choices.why: Both trends are reversed. A higher bond order means a shorter bond (1.54 → 1.20 Å for carbon) and a stronger one (348 → 839 kJ/mol).

explanation: As more electrons are shared, the bond order rises, the bond gets stronger and the nuclei move closer. For nitrogen, N–N, N=N and N≡N go from 163 to 418 to 941 kJ/mol, while the length falls from 1.47 to 1.24 to 1.10 Å.

prompt: Table 9.10.1 lists a bond enthalpy of 163 kJ/mol for N–N (bond order 1) and 941 kJ/mol for N≡N (bond order 3). How many times larger is the N≡N bond enthalpy than the N–N bond enthalpy?
explanation: 941 kJ/mol ÷ 163 kJ/mol = 5.77. Tripling the bond order makes the nitrogen–nitrogen bond almost six times stronger, so bond strength rises steeply with bond order.

prompt: In Example 9.10.1, the valence electrons of O2 fill σ_2s, σ_2s^* and σ_2pz first. Where do the next four electrons go?

choices.text: Into the two bonding π orbitals
Into the two antibonding π^* orbitals
choices.why: The bonding π orbitals are lower in energy and fill first. Only the last two of O2's 12 valence electrons go into π^*.

choices.text: Into the σ_2pz^* antibonding orbital
choices.why: σ_2pz^* is the highest valence orbital and stays empty in O2. The four electrons fill the bonding π_2px and π_2py pair.

choices.text: Two into π orbitals, two into π^*
choices.why: The bonding π pair holds four electrons and fills completely before any electron enters π^*.

explanation: After 6 electrons fill σ_2s, σ_2s^* and σ_2pz, the next 4 fill the degenerate bonding π_2px and π_2py orbitals. Only the last 2 of the 12 valence electrons go into the π^* pair.

prompt: In Example 9.10.1, which rule puts the last two valence electrons of O2 in separate π^* orbitals with parallel spins?

choices.text: Hund's first rule
The Pauli exclusion principle
choices.why: Pauli only limits an orbital to two electrons of opposite spin; it would allow both in one π^* orbital. Hund's first rule favors separate orbitals with parallel spins.

choices.text: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation
choices.why: That separates nuclear and electronic motion; it says nothing about how electrons fill degenerate orbitals. Hund's first rule does.

choices.text: Filling the lowest orbital first
choices.why: The two π^* orbitals have the same energy, so filling lowest-first can't choose between them. Hund's first rule spreads the electrons out with parallel spins.

explanation: The π_2px^* and π_2py^* orbitals are degenerate. Hund's first rule says the arrangement with the highest spin is the most stable, so one electron goes into each, with parallel spins.

prompt: In which orbitals are the two unpaired electrons of O2?

choices.text: One in each of the two π^* orbitals
One in each of the two bonding π orbitals
choices.why: The bonding π orbitals are full, with four paired electrons. The unpaired electrons are in the antibonding π^* pair.

choices.text: Both in the σ_2pz^* orbital
choices.why: σ_2pz^* is empty in O2, and two electrons sharing one orbital would have to be paired anyway.

choices.text: One in σ_2s^* and one in π^*
choices.why: σ_2s^* is full, with two paired electrons. The unpaired electrons are the last two, in π_2px^* and π_2py^*.

explanation: O2's last two valence electrons go one each into π_2px^* and π_2py^*. These are antibonding orbitals, so they count against the bond: (8 − 4)/2 = 2.

prompt: Example 9.10.1 compares MO theory with experiment: O2 has a bond length of 120.7 pm and a bond energy of 498.4 kJ/mol. What do these values support?

choices.text: The predicted bond order of 2, a double bond
A bond order of 3, like the N≡N triple bond
choices.why: N≡N is shorter and far stronger (1.10 Å, 941 kJ/mol). O2's values fit the double bond that a bond order of 2 predicts.

choices.text: A bond order of 1, a single bond
choices.why: A single O–O bond is much longer, as in O_2^2− at 149 pm. O2's 120.7 pm fits a double bond.

choices.text: The presence of two unpaired electrons
choices.why: Bond length and bond energy follow the bond order, not the spins. The unpaired electrons show up in O2's attraction to a magnet.

explanation: MO theory gives O2 a bond order of (8 − 4)/2 = 2. The measured bond length of 120.7 pm and bond energy of 498.4 kJ/mol agree with a double bond.

prompt: Example 9.10.1 writes the full configuration of O2, core included, as (σ_1s)^2(σ_1s^*)^2(σ_2s)^2(σ_2s^*)^2(σ_2pz)^2(π_2px)^2(π_2py)^2(π_2px^*)^1(π_2py^*)^1. How many of these electrons are in bonding orbitals?
explanation: The bonding orbitals are σ_1s, σ_2s, σ_2pz, π_2px and π_2py, with 2 electrons each: 5 × 2 = 10. The other 6 are antibonding, so the bond order is (10 − 6)/2 = 2, the same as from the valence electrons alone, because the full σ_1s and σ_1s^* pair cancels.

prompt: Suppose the two π^* electrons of O2 were paired in one π^* orbital instead of spread over two. What would happen to the bond order?

choices.text: It would still be 2
It would rise to 3
choices.why: Pairing doesn't move any electron out of an antibonding orbital. There are still 8 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons, so (8 − 4)/2 = 2.

choices.text: It would fall to 1
choices.why: The counts don't change: 8 bonding and 4 antibonding electrons still give (8 − 4)/2 = 2.

choices.text: It would become 2.5
choices.why: A half-integer needs an odd difference between bonding and antibonding counts. Pairing leaves 8 and 4, so the bond order stays 2.

explanation: Bond order depends only on how many electrons are in bonding and antibonding orbitals, (8 − 4)/2 = 2 either way. What would change is the magnetism: with the spins paired, O2 would have no unpaired electrons.

prompt: Which valence configuration is correct for O_2^−?

choices.why: That is neutral O2, with 12 valence electrons. O_2^− has one more, so π^* holds 3.
The bonding π orbitals fill before π^*. With 13 electrons, π holds 4 and π^* holds 3.
σ_2pz^* is higher in energy than π^*, and the π^* pair still has room. The 13th electron goes into π^*.

explanation: O_2^− has 6 + 6 + 1 = 13 valence electrons. After σ_2s, σ_2s^*, σ_2pz and the two bonding π orbitals take 10, the last 3 go into the degenerate π^* pair.

prompt: O_2^− has 8 electrons in bonding valence orbitals and 5 in antibonding valence orbitals. Using bond order = (n_b − n_a)/2, where n_b and n_a are the numbers of bonding and antibonding electrons, what is the bond order of O_2^−? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: Bond order = (8 − 5)/2 = 3/2 = 1.5. That is between a single and a double bond, so the O_2^− bond (128 pm) is longer than in O2 (121 pm) but shorter than in O_2^2− (149 pm).

prompt: The valence configuration of O_2^+ is (σ_2s)^2(σ_2s^*)^2(σ_2pz)^2(π_2px)^2(π_2py)^2(π_2px^*)^1(π_2py^*)^0. How many unpaired electrons does O_2^+ have?
explanation: Every orbital is doubly occupied except π_2px^*, which holds 1 electron, so O_2^+ has 1 unpaired electron. Like O2, it is paramagnetic, but with one unpaired electron instead of two.

prompt: The section gives two equally valid configurations for O_2^+, one ending (π_2px^*)^1(π_2py^*)^0 and one ending (π_2px^*)^0(π_2py^*)^1. Why are both valid?

choices.text: π_2px^* and π_2py^* have the same energy
The two configurations give different bond orders
choices.why: Both have 8 bonding and 3 antibonding electrons, so both give 2.5. They are equally valid because the two π^* orbitals are degenerate.

choices.text: The electron is split, half in each orbital
choices.why: Each configuration puts the whole electron in one orbital. Either orbital will do because the two have the same energy.

choices.text: The π^* orbitals are nonbonding in O_2^+
choices.why: They are antibonding, as in O2. The two configurations are equally good because π_2px^* and π_2py^* are degenerate.

explanation: The π_2px^* and π_2py^* orbitals are degenerate, so O_2^+'s single π^* electron can sit in either one with the same energy. The same goes for the one half-empty π^* orbital of O_2^−.

prompt: O_2^+ (112.2 pm) has a shorter bond than O2 (121 pm). Why does removing an electron shorten the bond?

choices.text: The lost electron was antibonding
The lost electron was bonding
choices.why: Losing a bonding electron would lower the bond order and lengthen the bond. The electron comes from π^*, so the bond order rises from 2 to 2.5.

choices.text: The positive charge pulls the two nuclei together
choices.why: Both nuclei are positive, so extra positive charge doesn't pull them together. The bond shortens because an antibonding electron is lost.

choices.text: Fewer electrons always give a shorter bond
choices.why: Not always: removing a bonding electron makes a bond longer. Here the electron removed is antibonding, so the bond order goes up.

explanation: O2's highest-energy electrons are in π^*. Removing one leaves 8 bonding and 3 antibonding electrons, so the bond order rises from 2 to 2.5 and the bond becomes stronger and shorter.

prompt: Adding one electron to a π^* orbital raises the number of antibonding electrons, n_a, by 1. Using bond order = (n_b − n_a)/2, by how much does the bond order drop for each electron added to π^*? (Give it as a decimal.)
explanation: One more antibonding electron lowers n_b − n_a by 1, so the bond order drops by 1/2 = 0.5. That is why it falls in steps of 0.5 from O_2^+ (2.5) to O2 (2), O_2^− (1.5) and O_2^2− (1).

prompt: MO theory gives O_2^+ a bond order of 2.5. How can a bond order be a half-integer?

choices.text: n_b − n_a can be an odd number
The bond flips between a double and a triple bond
choices.why: No flipping is needed. With bond order = (n_b − n_a)/2, an odd difference simply gives a half-integer.

choices.text: The bond order is rounded from a computed energy
choices.why: Bond order is an exact count, (n_b − n_a)/2, not a rounded energy. It is a half-integer whenever n_b − n_a is odd.

choices.text: One atom shares only half an electron
choices.why: Electrons aren't split in half. O_2^+ has 8 bonding and 3 antibonding electrons, and (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5.

explanation: Bond order = (n_b − n_a)/2 counts single electrons, not only pairs. O_2^+ has n_b − n_a = 8 − 3 = 5, an odd number, so its bond order is 2.5; O_2^− likewise has 1.5.

prompt: Example 9.10.1 ranks four oxygen species by bond length. Which order, from shortest to longest bond, does MO theory predict?

choices.why: This is reversed. Each added electron goes into π^* and lowers the bond order, so the bond gets longer from O_2^+ to O_2^2−.
O_2^+ has a higher bond order (2.5) than O2 (2), so its bond is shorter: 112.2 pm against 121 pm.
O_2^2− has the lowest bond order, 1, so it has the longest bond (149 pm), longer than O_2^− (128 pm).

explanation: The bond orders are 2.5, 2, 1.5 and 1, so the bond lengthens in the order O_2^+ < O2 < O_2^− < O_2^2−. Experiment agrees: 112.2, 121, 128 and 149 pm.

prompt: The measured O–O bond length is 112.2 pm in O_2^+ and 149 pm in O_2^2−. How much longer is the bond in O_2^2− than in O_2^+, in pm?
explanation: 149 pm − 112.2 pm = 36.8 pm. The three extra π^* electrons in O_2^2− lower the bond order from 2.5 to 1, so the bond is much longer.

prompt: Example 9.10.1 gives O2 a bond energy of 498.4 kJ/mol. Using 96.49 kJ/mol = 1 eV per molecule, what is this bond energy in eV per molecule?
explanation: 498.4 kJ/mol ÷ 96.49 kJ/mol per eV = 5.17 eV. That is the energy needed to break the double bond in one O2 molecule.

prompt: Which of the four oxygen species in Example 9.10.1 is not paramagnetic?

choices.text: O2
choices.why: O2 has two unpaired π^* electrons, so it is paramagnetic. O_2^2− fills both π^* orbitals and pairs every electron.
O_2^+ has one unpaired electron in π^*, so it is paramagnetic. Only O_2^2− has all its electrons paired.
O_2^− has three π^* electrons, one of them unpaired. O_2^2− has four, all paired.

explanation: O_2^2− ends in (π_2px^*)^2(π_2py^*)^2, so all of its electrons are paired and it is not drawn into a magnetic field. O2 has two unpaired electrons, and O_2^+ and O_2^− have one each.

prompt: What does it mean to say that O2 is paramagnetic?

choices.text: It is drawn into a magnetic field
It is pushed out of a magnetic field
choices.why: That is the opposite. O2 is attracted into the field, because of its unpaired electrons.

choices.text: It is a permanent magnet on its own
choices.why: O2 is not a magnet by itself; it is attracted only when a field is applied. That attraction is paramagnetism.

choices.text: It is not affected by a magnetic field
choices.why: Many substances barely respond, but O2 is pulled into the field. That is what paramagnetic means.

explanation: A paramagnetic substance is attracted into a magnetic field. In O2 the attraction comes from its two unpaired electrons.

prompt: What happens to liquid oxygen placed between the poles of a powerful magnet?

choices.text: It stays held between the poles
It flows straight past the poles
choices.why: That is what most liquids do. Liquid O2 is pulled into the field and held between the poles until it evaporates.

choices.text: It freezes solid between the poles
choices.why: The magnet doesn't cool the oxygen. The liquid stays suspended between the poles until it boils away.

choices.text: It is pushed away from the poles
choices.why: O2 is attracted into the field, not repelled, so it stays suspended between the poles.

explanation: Because O2 has two unpaired electrons, it is paramagnetic and is attracted into the magnetic field. Liquid O2 remains suspended between the poles of a strong magnet until it boils away.

prompt: Why are most substances not attracted into a magnetic field the way liquid O2 is?

choices.text: Their electrons are all paired
Their molecules have no π orbitals
choices.why: Many molecules have filled π orbitals; O2 itself has a full bonding π pair. The attraction needs unpaired electrons, not π orbitals.

choices.text: They contain too many electrons
choices.why: The total number of electrons doesn't decide it. What matters is whether any electrons are unpaired.

choices.text: Their bonds are only single bonds
choices.why: Bond order doesn't decide it. O2 is attracted because it has unpaired electrons, while most substances have only paired electrons.

explanation: Paramagnetism comes from unpaired electrons. Most substances have only paired electrons, so they are not drawn into a magnetic field; O2, with two unpaired electrons, is.

prompt: Which bonding model predicts that O2 has two unpaired electrons?

choices.text: Molecular orbital theory
Lewis electron-dot structures
choices.why: A Lewis structure pairs all of O2's electrons. Only MO theory predicts the two unpaired electrons.

choices.text: Valence bond theory
choices.why: The section says valence bond theory can't predict O2's unpaired electrons. MO theory can.

choices.text: None; they are known only from experiment
choices.why: MO theory predicts them: the last two electrons go into separate π^* orbitals. That explained a long-standing puzzle.

explanation: None of the other bonding models, such as valence bond theory or Lewis structures, can predict the two unpaired electrons. MO theory does, which explained why liquid O2 is attracted to a magnet: one of the earliest triumphs of MO theory.

prompt: A Lewis structure and MO theory both give O2 a double bond. On what do they disagree?

choices.text: Whether O2 has unpaired electrons
How many valence electrons O2 has
choices.why: Both count 12 valence electrons, 6 from each O atom. They differ on whether every electron is paired.

choices.text: How strong the O–O bond should be
choices.why: Both give a double bond, so both expect about the same strength. The difference is that MO theory leaves two electrons unpaired.

choices.text: Whether the two O atoms share electrons
choices.why: Both describe a covalent bond with shared electrons. They disagree about whether all of O2's electrons are paired.

explanation: The Lewis structure O=O pairs every electron, so it predicts no attraction to a magnet. MO theory gives the same bond order of 2 but puts two electrons in separate π^* orbitals with parallel spins, matching the observed paramagnetism.

prompt: What is a spin barrier, as described at the end of the section?

choices.text: The energy cost of flipping an electron's spin in a reaction
The energy needed to pair two electrons in one orbital
choices.why: The barrier isn't about pairing within an orbital. It is the large energy cost of changing an electron's spin as O2 reacts to give products with only paired electrons.

choices.text: The magnetic force that holds liquid O2 between magnet poles
choices.why: That is paramagnetism. A spin barrier is the energy cost of changing an electron's spin during a reaction.

choices.text: The energy released when O2 reacts with organic compounds
choices.why: That reaction energy is released, since the reaction is exothermic. The spin barrier is the large energy input a spin change needs, which slows the reaction.

explanation: Reactions of O2 with organic compounds to give H2O, CO2 and N2 would require at least one electron on O2 to change its spin. This needs a large input of energy, an obstacle chemists call a spin barrier.

prompt: In the reaction of O2 with organic compounds to give H2O, CO2 and N2, which substance has unpaired electrons?

choices.text: O2
H2O
choices.why: Like nearly all organic compounds, H2O has only paired electrons. O2 alone has two unpaired electrons.

choices.text: CO2
choices.why: CO2 has only paired electrons. The odd one out is O2, with two unpaired electrons.

choices.text: N2
choices.why: N2 has only paired electrons. O2 is the only species in the reaction with unpaired electrons.

explanation: Organic compounds and the products H2O, CO2 and N2 all have only paired electrons, but O2 has two unpaired electrons. That mismatch is what creates the spin barrier.

prompt: Why does the section call the magnetic properties of O2 crucial to the existence of life?

choices.text: They keep tissues from reacting fast with air
They let O2 bind to the iron atoms in hemoglobin
choices.why: The section doesn't discuss hemoglobin. Its point is that the spin barrier makes organic matter react only very slowly with air.

choices.text: They let living cells react with O2 very quickly
choices.why: The section says the opposite: the spin barrier makes the reaction of organic compounds with O2 very slow.

choices.text: They keep O2 from dissolving in water or blood
choices.why: Solubility isn't the point. O2's unpaired electrons create a spin barrier that keeps tissues from reacting rapidly with air.

explanation: With 20% O2 in the air, organic compounds, including body tissues, should react rapidly and exothermically to give H2O, CO2 and N2. They don't, because the reaction would need an electron to change its spin. This spin barrier makes it very, very slow.

prompt: The reaction of organic compounds with O2 releases energy. What does the spin barrier change about this reaction?

choices.text: Only how fast it happens
It makes the reaction absorb energy
choices.why: The reaction is still exothermic. The barrier is an energy input needed along the way, so it only slows the reaction down.

choices.text: It changes which products form
choices.why: The products are still H2O, CO2 and N2. The barrier only makes the reaction very slow.

choices.text: It stops the reaction from ever happening
choices.why: The reaction can still happen; it is just very, very slow, because an electron must change its spin.

explanation: The reaction to H2O, CO2 and N2 stays exothermic. The spin barrier is a large energy cost along the way, so it makes the reaction very slow without changing its products or the energy it releases.
